newsitem.title: USA: CFTC's Born fears liquidity problem in ag markets.
newsitem.headline: CFTC's Born fears liquidity problem in ag markets.

text.p: Commodities Futures Trading Commission chief Brooksley Born said Tuesday she was concerned that pending legislation to eliminate much of the agency's regulatory authority could hurt farmers and ranchers using the futures market.

"I'm very concerned that if this were a segregated market," Born said in testimony before a House Agriculture subcommittee, "speculative interest might leave the agricultural markets and go to the unregulated markets, reducing liquidity."

Born was speaking about a proposed House bill that would create so-called a "professional market" comprised of traders and individuals with $1 million in assets who would be exempt from CFTC regulations. The agency would still regulate smaller players in the U.S. futures market, who account for an estimated 10 percent of volume.
Speaking to reporters after the hearing, Born said that liquidity was not her only concern about the pending legislation.
"A single clearinghouse might put the regulated trades at some financial jeopardy," she said, referring to the proposed division between a professional market and the remaining players.
"The elimination of regulation that would occur under the Ewing bill would be inappropriate for these (agricultural) markets," she said.

But, she added that the CFTC "believes there should be some compromise between the elimination of regulation and the current pilot program." The pilot program was proposed by the CFTC several months ago as a way to work with the exchanges in speeding up approval of new contracts. To date, no exchange has put forward a pilot program proposal.
Born also said the CFTC staff continues to meet with exchange officials "to see if we can find a common ground on the professional markets."
But, she said during her testimony, that, "We have not had what I would consider meaningful discussions between the commission and the exchanges."
Born also said she was "a little dubious" that the exchanges would voluntarily provide data about large trader positions and audit trails if they did not have to by law.
Senior officials with the Chicago Board of Trade and the Chicago Mercantile Exchange were scheduled to meet with CFTC Commissioner Barbara Pedersen Holum.
